evals.prompt: I run BD at Threadline, a $14M ARR B2B workforce-scheduling SaaS. My exec team wants a shortlist of 5 integration partners for next year and I have a draft: Slack (our CTO knows their partner lead personally), Workday (biggest logo we could realistically land), Gusto (met their BD guy at a conference in May, we got on great), Notion (everyone integrates with Notion), and Rippling (a competitor announced one in March). For context: our CRM has a partner-source field that nobody fills in, sales win/loss notes mentioned missing payroll integrations about a dozen times last quarter, and support logged 40-something tickets asking for Gusto sync. Give me the partner strategy.
evals.expected_output: A partner-selection approach that gates the shortlist on written demand evidence, drops the relationship- and logo-driven candidates, proposes competing portfolio shapes before committing, and places survivors on the depth ladder at the default rung.
expectations: Asks clarifying questions before delivering a finished strategy, or explicitly gates the strategy on interview answers covering deadline, one-off-win vs compounding-asset, and effort ceiling
Requires every shortlisted partner to carry a written demand-evidence line (named deals, request counts, or retention data)
Rejects or parks the Notion and Workday candidates for having no demand evidence, rather than keeping them on the strength of ubiquity or logo size
Treats the conference relationship as non-evidence for Gusto, while keeping Gusto on the strength of the 40-odd support tickets and the payroll win/loss mentions
Names the three primary selection filters: customer and prospect demand, market/SAM expansion, and competitive necessity
Adds quantified signals including deal-attached revenue (dollar value of open deals blocked on each missing integration), ecosystem gravity, and retention/attach lift
Flags that the unfilled partner-source CRM field makes attribution plumbing a prerequisite rather than an afterthought
Proposes 2-3 candidate portfolio shapes with trade-offs (such as few-and-deep, category-coverage breadth, platform-anchor) and recommends one, instead of delivering a single finished list
Places selected partners on the five-rung depth ladder running referral, reseller, co-sell/integration alliance, co-build/strategic alliance, OEM/embed
Names co-sell/integration alliance as the default depth rung rather than opening every partner at a deep alliance
Recommends proving 1-3 partner types first before adding depth or more partners
Sets a recurring cadence of quarterly prioritization review with monthly intake from sales and CS

evals.prompt: Our CFO at Bellwright (HR-tech, roughly $40M ARR) killed the partnerships headcount request last quarter. His reason: our dashboard claimed partners touched $31M of revenue, which is more than three quarters of the entire company. That number comes from a Google Sheet our partner manager Dana updates in the last week of each quarter - she tags any closed-won deal where a partner logo appears anywhere in the opportunity notes. We are going back in Q3 to ask for three more heads. Rebuild the number so it survives finance.
evals.expected_output: An attribution rebuild that replaces the blended spreadsheet figure with two separate capped CRM-level numbers, claimed at deal creation with dated IDs, plus the comp, forecast, and reporting changes that make the data credible.
expectations: Splits reporting into two separate numbers, partner-sourced and partner-influenced, and refuses to report a single blended partner-touched figure
Defines sourced as a deal that would not exist without the partner, and influenced as a deal that already existed and the partner materially advanced
Caps influenced credit and explains that uncapped influence is how partner-attributed revenue comes to exceed total revenue
Moves attribution out of the spreadsheet onto a partner-source field on the CRM opportunity record
Requires attribution claimed at deal creation with a dated claim ID, never reverse-engineered at close
Identifies the conflict in having the number maintained by the person whose quota or headcount request depends on it
Specifies a short attribution window of roughly 14 days from deal creation
Limits credit to one sourced partner per deal
Requires credit caps set before the quarter starts rather than after results are known
Calls for equalizing AE compensation on partner deals, because AEs paid less on partner deals deprioritize them
Rolls partner pipeline into the same forecast review and the same exit criteria as direct pipeline
States that referral, co-sell, and OEM motions need different attribution rules rather than one generic scheme

Reports an executive KPI set inside dashboards leadership already checks - sourced vs influenced revenue, activation rate, time to first deal, partner CAC vs direct CAC - rather than a standalone partner report

evals.prompt: Quick one. We are Latchpoint, 60 people, field-service scheduling software. Two of our largest customers run NetSuite and two more run Salesforce. Sales says getting listed on AppExchange and earning the Built for NetSuite badge would unblock about $900K of stalled deals. I have exactly one integration engineer and a CFO who wants the full cost of both before he signs anything. What is the number, and should we do it?
evals.expected_output: A certification cost model that treats both programs as recurring standing engineering work with named owners, carries the concrete fee, timeline, and failure-rate figures, and tests the single-engineer constraint before recommending a join.
expectations: Treats certification as a recurring standing cost rather than a one-time launch project
States the AppExchange security review carries a $999 per-submission fee
States the AppExchange review takes roughly 6-9 weeks initially plus 2-3 weeks per resubmission
Warns that roughly half of first AppExchange submissions fail, and budgets at least one resubmission cycle
States that Built for NetSuite must be renewed at every major NetSuite release, twice yearly
Notes Built for NetSuite is revocable at any time the standards lapse
Names a renewal owner for each certification joined
Counts recurring certification maintenance against integration-engineer headcount and flags the single engineer as the binding constraint
Mentions Salesforce's ongoing listing cost of roughly $150/yr and/or its 15% revenue share, 25% for OEM
Tests each platform against whether it reaches a segment the demand evidence names, not only against the stalled deal value
Advises verifying current program requirements and tier names against each platform's own current documentation before committing
Requires the effort ceiling in engineering hours per quarter to be checked before joining rather than discovered afterwards

evals.prompt: Cassava Systems here, warehouse inventory software, about $22M ARR, all direct sales, no channel, and every contract is signed by us - finance flatly refuses to let another company be the transacting party on our revenue. Three partnership conversations are live right now. Kitewell, a robotics vendor: their reps sent us 6 opportunities over the last two quarters, 2 closed, and their largest customers keep asking for a real productized integration instead of the CSV hack we have. Norsefield, a large ERP: they want to white-label our forecasting module inside their product under their own brand, and they have floated minimum annual commitments. Orbit Freight, a TMS: interesting people, but zero customer overlap so far and nobody has ever asked us for it. Separately, our VP Sales wants to list on AWS Marketplace and keeps calling that the deepest tier of partnership. How deep do we go with each?
evals.expected_output: A per-partner placement on the five-rung ladder with graduation gates, the reseller rung deleted rather than parked, white-label distinguished from OEM, and the cloud-marketplace framing corrected.
expectations: Places each partner on the five-rung ladder: referral, reseller, co-sell/integration alliance, co-build/strategic alliance, OEM/embed
Promotes Kitewell toward co-build/strategic alliance, citing already-sourced pipeline plus joint-customer pull for a productized integration
Places Orbit Freight at referral or parks it, because no demand evidence exists yet
Deletes the reseller rung outright rather than demoting or parking it, because the business cannot support partner-transacted deals
Explains that a parked or merely demoted rung silently reappears as scope later
Distinguishes white-label from true OEM: white-label hides the vendor brand but typically carries no roadmap commitment, so it is its own category rather than a synonym
States that OEM/embed revenue share runs roughly 10-30% of the partner's revenue from the powered feature
Flags OEM/embed as the hardest rung to unwind once the partner's customers depend on it, with minimum commitments as a precondition for promotion
Corrects the AWS Marketplace framing: cloud-marketplace co-sell is a channel and transaction decision, not a depth rung on this ladder
Gates every graduation on proven joint economics plus the three-fit test, requiring product fit, commercial fit, and operational fit to line up simultaneously
Notes the co-build commitment shape: a 12-18 month joint roadmap with shared pipeline targets

Names the compliance cost each rung triggers, such as OEM licensing with IP and indemnity terms, a joint development agreement for co-build, NDA and revenue-share terms for co-sell, and referral being terminable at will
States the ranking is a default to be re-ranked against the deadline, one-off-vs-compounding, and effort-ceiling answers

evals.prompt: Meridian Loop, 38 employees, SaaS for clinical trial site management. We just hired our first dedicated partnerships person, Priya. Our COO wants to stand her up as VP of a proper Alliances org with a partner ops hire and a partner marketer underneath her, so that partnerships finally gets the respect it needs internally. Today partnerships informally sits with our head of sales. We have 4 integrations live and none of them produces measurable pipeline yet. Where should this function live, and what do we staff?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to keep the function under Sales at this stage, with the standalone Alliances org named as the deliberately starved option, the ~100-employee split threshold, the Product migration condition, and attribution plumbing built now.
expectations: Recommends keeping the function reporting into Sales at this stage rather than standing up a standalone Alliances org

Names the standalone Alliances org as the highest-value and highest-cost option that an efficiency ranking never picks, and states the condition that promotes it anyway, such as partner-sourced revenue becoming a board-level metric or deep-rung governance needing dedicated owners
Notes that reporting into Sales costs zero reorganization and keeps an unproven function tied to revenue
Ties the recommendation to the fact that none of the 4 live integrations produces measurable pipeline yet, so the function is still unproven
Names roughly the 100-employee mark as the threshold for splitting into dedicated roles, well above the current 38
Describes the split-role shape at that threshold: partner/alliance manager plus a partner or integration engineer plus an integration product manager
Recommends treating the top 10-15 partners as named strategic accounts once the split happens
Names the condition for migrating integrations under Product: when productizing integrations becomes the goal, so they get built for scale instead of as bespoke BD favors
Prescribes building the attribution plumbing during this Sales-reporting phase, before the program scales
Ranks the three placements explicitly on effort, value, and efficiency instead of presenting them as a flat list of options

evals.prompt: We signed a strategic alliance with Halvard Analytics six months ago and our two products are supposed to ship a deep joint integration. Since kickoff we have had exactly two calls, both of which were them presenting slides about their quarterly numbers and us presenting ours. Their engineering team went quiet around month three and we only found out from a mutual customer last week that they had re-platformed their API. Our legal team is now asking whether we should have set this up as a joint venture. Fix the governance.
evals.expected_output: A governance rebuild that reclassifies the calls as status updates, specifies real QBR mechanics with resource-approving attendees, installs shared roadmap visibility and a joint business plan, and recommends a scoped JDA over a joint venture.
expectations: Diagnoses the two calls as status updates rather than QBRs, because they produced no dated commitments
Specifies a QBR as a working session reviewing last quarter against the previous QBR's commitments and setting the next quarter's
Requires someone on each side who can approve resources to be present at the QBR
Requires roadmap visibility shared from the start rather than at launch, so a partner re-platform surfaces before a customer reports it
Sets a sync cadence of at least quarterly covering integration performance, upcoming platform changes, and customer feedback
Recommends a joint development agreement scoped to the specific integration, with IP, support, and roadmap terms explicit, rather than a joint venture
Explains that a joint venture creates a new jointly-owned legal entity and should be reserved for a genuinely shared new entity or product
Requires a joint business plan with shared targets on a timeline and an explicit statement of which side carries the heavier lift at each phase, so a stall obligates the other side to unblock
Reframes the integration as a product with its own roadmap, quality bar, security review, and definition of done, instead of a project
Warns that project framing makes post-launch decay the default outcome

evals.prompt: Building the board deck for our partnerships review at Ferncastle (DevOps tooling, $18M ARR). Two things I want checked before it goes out. First, my Salesforce slide says we should target Crest tier and eventually Summit on their ISV partner program, and my Atlassian slide has Silver/Gold/Platinum with a note that Gold needs $500K in cloud sales. Second, the headline stat on slide 2 is that 83% of enterprise buyers cite integrations as a purchase-decision factor, and slide 9 says ecosystem-qualified deals are 53% more likely to close and close 46% faster. Sanity check this for me.
evals.expected_output: A correction pass that replaces the deprecated Salesforce tiers with the current journey stages, fixes the Atlassian threshold and its security requirement, and relabels both cited statistics with their real sourcing strength.
expectations: Flags Base/Ridge/Crest/Summit as Salesforce's retired legacy Trailblazer-Score ISV tiers, replaced in July 2024
Gives the current Salesforce ISV journey stages: Registered, Exploration, Build, Select, Summit
Corrects the Atlassian Gold threshold to $750K in cloud sales, and gives Silver at $150K and Platinum at $3M
Notes that Atlassian Gold and above additionally require SOC 2 Type 2 or ISO 27001
Labels the 83% enterprise-buyers figure as circulated without a traceable primary study, and advises against presenting it to a CFO or board as a cited benchmark
Labels the 53% and 46% ecosystem-qualified-deal figures as vendor-published and drawn from top-performing cohorts, so they read as directional ceilings rather than median outcomes
Advises measuring Ferncastle's own program with its own attribution data instead of leading the deck with industry-wide lift figures
Recommends verifying every tier name against the platform's own current documentation before the deck ships, since third-party guides still describe deprecated tiers
Notes that the 2024-2026 period was a restructuring wave that renamed tiers across nearly every major platform
